hops.title: True Blue and the visual neurons that once reached for the spinal cord
hops.text: In 1982, Brent Stanfield, Dennis O'Leary and C. Fricks were mapping which cortical neurons send axons down the pyramidal tract toward the spinal cord. They injected a fluorescent tracer called True Blue where that tract crosses in the brainstem. In rats in their first week of life, labeled neurons turned up across nearly the whole neocortex, visual cortex included. In adult rats, the same injection labels none there. So did the young visual neurons die? The team injected in week one and looked again at week four. The blue cells were still sitting in visual cortex. They had lived and dropped only the branch headed for the spinal cord.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A white laboratory rat sitting on a wooden bench beside a cobalt-blue glass vial in daylight.
image.caption: Young rat visual neurons send a branch toward the spinal cord, then drop the branch and keep living.

hops.title: Why eye doctors patch a child's stronger eye
hops.text: When amblyopia affects one eye in childhood, the brain comes to rely on the stronger eye while vision in the weaker eye falls behind. After addressing any underlying vision problem, one clinician-directed treatment patches the stronger eye so the brain uses the weaker one. In 1993, Antonella Antonini and Michael Stryker closed one eye in kittens during the critical period and traced single thalamic axon arbors in visual cortex. Branches relaying the deprived eye's input withdrew rapidly. A 2003 trial of 189 children under seven with moderate amblyopia found that shorter and longer daily patching schedules, each with close-up tasks, gave similar vision gains at four months.

sources.citation: Repka et al. (Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group), Arch. Ophthalmol. 121:603-611 (2003)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A smiling young child wearing a patterned cloth eye patch over one eye, assembling a wooden puzzle at a sunny table.
image.caption: Patching makes the brain use the weaker eye; in kittens, thalamic axon branches carrying deprived-eye input withdraw in cortex.

hops.title: Moths that remember what they learned as caterpillars
hops.text: A common picture is that metamorphosis wipes a caterpillar's nervous system clean. In 2008, Georgetown biologists tested whether a learned odor aversion survives metamorphosis. They paired ethyl acetate with a mild electric shock in late-stage tobacco hornworms; 78 percent then avoided the odor in a Y-shaped choice apparatus. About a month later, 77 percent of adult moths still avoided it. In a separate carryover test, scrubbing trained caterpillars' pupal cases with a soft brush and distilled water did not erase the aversion. Caterpillars trained earlier, as third instars, showed no clear preference as adults. That fits early-born fly gamma neurons pruning larval branches, though this study did not test it.

sources.citation: Blackiston, Silva Casey & Weiss, PLoS ONE 3:e1736 (2008)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A green tobacco hornworm caterpillar and an adult hawkmoth beside a clear Y-shaped tunnel on a sunny greenhouse bench.
image.caption: Metamorphosis does not wipe the slate: moths keep an odor lesson learned late in caterpillar life.
